kurz: Why a bet with a positive expected value can ruin the individual with certainty, and what follows from this for leverage, concentration and insurance.

bloecke.md:
In fund prospectuses, pension calculators and newspaper articles, the word “average” refers to two different figures. The statement “7% on average” can mean that a thousand investors follow the same strategy for one year and their mean result is 7%. It can also mean that a single investor who sticks with the strategy for thirty years increases their wealth by 7% a year. The first figure is a cross-section across many investors, the second a longitudinal section through the life of a single investor.

A process in which both figures coincide is called **ergodic**. Rolling dice for fixed euro amounts is ergodic. Whether a hundred people roll once or one person rolls a hundred times, the mean per roll is the same, because the results add up. Wealth, by contrast, grows multiplicatively, because each return acts on what was left after the previous one. Multiplicative processes are not ergodic, and the difference between the two figures can be considerable.

eintraege.text: Average across many parallel paths at a single point in time. It corresponds to the ordinary expected value.
Growth rate that a single path shows over many periods. In multiplicative processes, it is the geometric mean of the factors.

bloecke.md:
The stake is €10,000. Round after round, the entire wealth is staked on the toss of a fair coin:

- Heads brings +50%, turning 10,000 into €15,000.
- Tails brings −40%, turning 10,000 into €6,000.

The expected value after one round is 0.5 × 15,000 + 0.5 × 6,000 = €10,500, that is, +5% per round.

After two rounds there are four equally likely paths ending at €22,500, €9,000, €9,000 and €3,600. Their mean is €11,025, exactly 10,000 × 1.05². Three of the four paths are below the stake. The average is calculated correctly but describes none of the four paths.

For the single path, what counts is the geometric mean of the factors: √(1.5 × 0.6) = √0.9 = 0.9487, that is, −5.1% per round. The same game therefore has an expected value of +5% and a growth rate of −5.1%.

bloecke.titel: Ensemble average and typical single path in the coin toss game
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation over 50 rounds starting at €10,000, logarithmic axis. The average of all players grows by 5% per round, while the typical single path loses 5.1% per round.

bloecke.md: The average rises even though almost all players lose, because it is determined by a few extreme paths. After 100 rounds, the ensemble average stands at €1.315 million (10,000 × 1.05¹⁰⁰, 131.5 times the stake). The path with exactly 50 heads ends at €52. The stake is only regained from 56 heads onwards, and the probability of this is just under 14%. Around three quarters of the ensemble average comes from paths with 61 to 74 heads, which together only 1.8% of players reach. Another quarter comes from paths with 75 or more heads, whose probability is below one in a million. The expected value is therefore of no use as a forecast of your own result.

bloecke.titel: Players above and below the starting capital after 100 rounds
bloecke.unter: Binomial calculation for 100 fair tosses. The starting capital is only regained from 56 heads onwards, and the majority of players do not manage this, even though the expected value per round is positive.

bloecke.md: The expected value is a statement about a collective, whereas your own portfolio is a single path. Investors who confuse the two are drawn to strategies that are highly likely to ruin them.

## Ruin as an absorbing barrier

Another reason why the average does not apply to the individual is that the process can end. A state that you can no longer leave is called an **absorbing barrier**. Zero is absorbing, because zero times any return remains zero. When you average over many parallel paths, one investor falling to zero is offset by another doubling their wealth. On a single path there is no such offsetting, because no further results follow after ruin.

In practice, the barrier is rarely at zero. It lies wherever you have to stop. This can be the bank's demand for additional collateral that closes out a securities-backed loan at the worst possible moment, a job loss that ends the monthly contributions, or the date on which the money is needed for a down payment. Each of these barriers ends the path before the average can materialise.

For contracts for difference (CFDs), an obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht) is prohibited for retail clients, and leverage is capped, from 30:1 for major currency pairs to 2:1 for crypto assets (product intervention by BaFin, the Federal Financial Supervisory Authority, under Section 15 WpHG, Securities Trading Act; European basis: Article 42 MiFIR). Bank balances are protected up to €100,000 per institution and customer (Section 8 EinSiG, Deposit Guarantee Act). Securities in a securities account belong to the customer in any case. With Lombard or property loans, it is possible to fall below zero. Such debtors get back to zero after three years through the discharge of residual debt (Restschuldbefreiung) under Section 287(2) InsO (Insolvency Code). All three rules ensure that the path can continue.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula derives the growth rate that a single path achieves over time from the expected return and the fluctuation. The deduction σ²/2 is called variance drain. It is neither a fee nor an error. It arises because returns are multiplied and not added.
variablen: growth rate of the single path (geometric)
bloecke.beispiel: For μ = 8% and σ = 20%, this gives g ≈ 0.08 − 0.04/2 = 0.06, that is, 6% instead of 8%. The approximation applies to lognormal returns and becomes inaccurate for very large σ, but this does not change the direction.

bloecke.titel: Same expected return, different fluctuation (illustrative calculation, μ = 8%, 30 years, €10,000, excluding costs and taxes)

bloecke.md:
## Leverage and growth rate

The formula answers the question of leverage before any market assessment comes into play. Leverage L multiplies the expected return by L, and the fluctuation as well. In the formula, however, the fluctuation is squared. For μ = 8% and σ = 20%, the result before costs is:

- unleveraged: 8 − 2 = 6%
- threefold: 24 − 18 = 6%
- fourfold: 32 − 32 = 0%
- fivefold: 40 − 50 = −10%

An investor with threefold leverage achieves the same growth rate as an unleveraged one, but has to accept setbacks three times as large. With fourfold leverage the growth rate is zero, and above that it turns negative. Financing costs, spreads and the daily rebalancing of leveraged products are not included. They push the threshold down. The calculation already assumes a positive expected value. It therefore describes the case in which the investor's market assessment turns out to be right.

If a position with a 25% portfolio weight falls to zero, the portfolio loses 25%. It then needs +33% to get back to 100. With a 50% weight, it needs +100%. The expected value of this position may have been very good. For the risk, it is enough that there is an outcome from which the position can no longer recover. Individual shares have such an outcome, a broad index practically does not, because it replaces its constituents instead of holding them until they suffer a total loss.

Taxation reinforces the asymmetry, because tax law also looks at each investor individually and does not average over parallel paths. On a €30,000 gain from share sales, once the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) has been used up, 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus the solidarity surcharge is due, together 26.375% or €7,912.50 (Section 32d(1) EStG, Income Tax Act; Section 4 SolzG 1995, Solidarity Surcharge Act). A €30,000 loss from share sales, by contrast, goes into the share loss pot (Aktienverlusttopf). It may only be offset against gains from share sales in the same year or in later years, that is, neither against dividends and interest nor against other types of income (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). The state receives a quarter of the gain immediately, but only shares in the loss if gains from share sales arise in the same year or later. An investor who stops after the loss keeps a loss carryforward that is worth nothing. The former cap of €20,000 a year on loss offsetting for derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) was abolished by the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz).

## Return gap between funds and investors

In its study “Mind the Gap”, Morningstar compares the return of funds with the average return on the money invested in them. In the decade to 31 December 2025, the funds achieved 9.9% a year and the investors 8.7%. The difference of 1.2 percentage points arises solely from the timing and size of purchases and sales. The gap is smallest where there is little fluctuation and largest where there is a lot. For crypto ETFs, from the start of 2024 to the end of 2025, it was around 14 points, 22% against 36% a year.

This gap must be distinguished from variance drain. It arises from investor behaviour, whereas variance drain is purely arithmetical. The gap is also disputed. Writing in the Financial Analysts Journal in 2026, Fulkerson, Jordan, Riley and Yan counter that the real damage from timing is considerably smaller. Both effects work in the same direction. The return of a fund and the return of its investors are therefore two different quantities.

bloecke.titel: Fund return minus investor return, decade to the end of 2025
bloecke.unter: Morningstar “Mind the Gap” 2026, gap in percentage points a year. For the most volatile fifth of funds, the analysis shows more than 2.0 points. Crypto ETFs are missing from the chart because their gap of around 14 points exceeds the scale.

bloecke.md:
## Insurance and diversification

If fluctuation lowers the time average, then anything that removes fluctuation and risks of ruin raises the time average, even if it costs expected value. From the insured person's point of view, personal liability insurance has a negative expected value. The premium is above the expected loss, otherwise there would be no insurers. Taking out the policy is nevertheless rational, because liability under Section 823 BGB (Civil Code) is unlimited in amount and a single case of personal injury ends the path. The same argument justifies the emergency fund, insuring your ability to work and diversification across hundreds of securities. In the ensemble these measures are expensive, on the single path they are cheap.

This also makes it impossible to maintain the view that risk-averse people are victims of their own psychology. Loss aversion is measurable. Across 607 estimates, the meta-analysis by Brown, Imai, Vieider and Camerer (2024) arrives at a factor of around 1.96. It is a bias where small, repeated, additive amounts are at stake. With multiplicative stakes and a barrier, on the other hand, caution is the right response.

1. Check the barrier first, then the return. Before every position, it is established what share of your wealth would be lost in the worst conceivable case rather than in the probable one.
2. Do not choose any structure in which a single event costs more than is available, and do not enter into any position whose total loss would wipe out several years' worth of saving.
3. Fluctuation is a deduction from return, not a price paid for it. If two routes lead to the same expected return, the calmer one is the better one for a single path.

Ergodicity economics is a young research programme (Ole Peters and others, since 2011) and is disputed among experts. It is an open question whether it replaces expected utility theory or merely reformulates what Daniel Bernoulli described in 1738 with diminishing marginal utility. In practice the dispute is secondary, because both theories advise avoiding risks of ruin.

The argument does not apply where stakes are small and practically additive. A lottery ticket does not change any wealth path. Nor does the argument justify taking no risk at all. Wealth held solely in an instant-access savings account faces a different, slower-acting problem on its path, namely inflation.

mitnehmen: The expected value describes many players at one point in time, the growth rate describes one player over many periods, and only the second figure applies to your own portfolio.
In multiplicative processes, fluctuation reduces the experienced return by approximately σ²/2 for the same expected return.
Events that end the process must not have any appreciable probability, regardless of how good the expected value looks.

Leverage acts linearly on the return and quadratically on the deduction, so the growth rate of any leveraged position turns negative above a certain factor, without any change in the prospects of the underlying.
Insurance and diversification lower the expected value but raise the time average, and that is where their benefit lies.

begriffe.text: Property of a random process in which the average across many parallel paths equals the average of a single path over time. Multiplicative wealth paths do not have this property.
Expected value across many parallel paths at a single point in time. This is the figure found in prospectuses and statistics.
Growth rate of a single path over many periods. For wealth, the time average is the geometric mean of the return factors.
State that a process never leaves once it has reached it. For wealth, this is ruin or any other point at which you have to get out.
Gap between the expected and the experienced return, approximately σ²/2. It arises solely because returns are multiplied.
